spec_used: specs/ocr/combined-science-b-21c-J260.md (+ combined-science-b-21c-J260-bold.md as the tier authority)

findings.claim: Key Fact: "Ionising radiation: alpha, beta and gamma from radioactive materials, plus X-rays. Non-ionising: UV, infrared, microwaves, radio waves."
findings.truth: High-energy ultraviolet is ionising. The list of non-ionising radiations should start with visible light, not UV.
findings.evidence: spec P1.1.7c: 'high energy ultraviolet, gamma rays and X-rays have enough energy to cause ionisation when absorbed by some atoms'. L3 of this same unit states the opposite ('UV, X-rays and gamma rays are ionising'), so the unit contradicted itself.

findings.claim: "Non-ionising radiation does not have enough energy to ionise atoms, though some forms (such as UV) can still cause harm at high doses."
findings.truth: The same misclassification of UV as non-ionising. The clause reads correctly with the UV example removed.
findings.evidence: spec P1.1.7c.

findings.claim: Match knowledge check, right option: "Weakly ionising, penetrates lead".
findings.truth: Gamma is absorbed by dense lead or thick concrete. The option as written teaches the opposite of the lesson's own text and would lose a mark if repeated.
findings.evidence: lesson content_html n7: 'only significantly absorbed by dense lead or thick concrete'.

findings.claim: Lesson 1 is titled 'Radiation: Risks and Benefits' (topic P1.1) but teaches alpha/beta/gamma penetration, contamination versus irradiation, half-life, tracers, sterilisation and smoke detectors.
findings.truth: That material is chapter P5 (Radioactive materials), topics P5.1 and P5.2. P1.1's own outcomes are the EM spectrum groupings (P1.1.1), the limited visible range (P1.1.2), the common finite speed (P1.1.3), absorption/transmission/reflection by wavelength (P1.1.5), electron arrangement and ionisation (P1.1.6), the generation table (P1.1.7a-e, including ozone), hazards (P1.1.8), uses (P1.1.9) and radio-wave oscillations (P1.1.10, Higher). L3 covers the spectrum, order, uses and hazards; the ozone point sits in L2. Options: (a) leave as taught, accepting P5 content arrives early, and check science-ocr-b/physics-paper-2 (queued, 8 lessons) for duplication before it is checked; (b) re-point L1 at P1.1 outcomes and move the P5 material to physics-paper-2. Recommend (a) plus a duplication check, because a rebuild would ripple through narration, podcasts and the widget map.
findings.evidence: spec P1.1 and P5.1/P5.2 assessable learning outcomes; queue entry science-ocr-b/physics-paper-2 exists and is still queued.

findings.claim: The paragraph explaining the greenhouse effect (surface emits infrared, greenhouse gases absorb and re-emit it, Earth would be far colder without them) is wrapped in a `higher-only` div.
findings.truth: The greenhouse-effect mechanism is assessed at both tiers, so the wrapper hid required content from Foundation students. The lesson's own untagged Key Fact, Key Takeaway, two knowledge checks and a 2-mark practice question all test it, so the page was internally inconsistent. Wrapper removed. The wrappers on the radiation-balance and albedo paragraphs are correct and were kept, because that reasoning is P1.2.2.
findings.evidence: spec C1.2.1 'describe the greenhouse effect in terms of the interaction of radiation with matter' is not bold; the P1.2 teaching narrative describing the greenhouse effect is not bold; only P1.2.2 (the incoming/absorbed/emitted balance) is bold.

findings.claim: Key Fact: "Greenhouse gases (CO2, CH2 = methane, water vapour)".
findings.truth: Methane is CH4. The entity used was ₂ (subscript two); it should be ₄ (subscript four).
findings.evidence: settled fact; spec P1.2 narrative names methane as a greenhouse gas.

findings.claim: Key Takeaway: "Greenhouse gases (CO2, CH2, water vapour) absorb outgoing infrared".
findings.truth: Methane is CH4.
findings.evidence: settled fact.

findings.claim: Answer key for the 3-mark question on why the atmosphere absorbs infrared but transmits visible light: "greenhouse gas molecules (CO2, CH2, H2O) ... the main atmospheric gases (N2 and O2) do not have vibrational modes at visible wavelengths, so they do not absorb visible light".
findings.truth: Two errors. Methane is CH4. And the reason N2 and O2 are transparent to the outgoing radiation is that they have no vibrational modes at INFRARED wavelengths, which is what the article itself says; no molecule has vibrational modes at visible wavelengths, so the stated reason is empty.
findings.evidence: settled fact; lesson content_html n10 states the correct reason.

findings.claim: Flashcard question: "What does Name three greenhouse gases state?"
findings.truth: A garbled drafting artefact. Rewritten as "Name three greenhouse gases.", which also satisfies the validator's opening-word rule.
findings.evidence: self-evident text corruption.

findings.claim: The whole reflection / refraction / diffraction bullet block is wrapped in a `higher-only` div.
findings.truth: Describing the effects of reflection and refraction at material interfaces is a both-tier outcome, so the wrapper hid required content. Only 'waves travel at different speeds in different substances' and 'explain how refraction is related to differences in speed' are Higher tier, and those two sentences cannot be split out without adding a narration block. The untagged Key Fact, a knowledge check and a 3-mark practice question all test this content, so the wrapper was removed.
findings.evidence: spec P1.3.8a is not bold; P1.3.9 and P1.3.10 are bold.

findings.claim: Flashcard question: "What fills in the blank: Cloze: wave speed = _____ x wavelength."
findings.truth: A garbled drafting artefact ('Cloze:' leaked from the generator). The answer is one word, so the question must open with 'What is'. Rewritten as "What is the missing quantity: wave speed = _____ x wavelength?"
findings.evidence: self-evident text corruption; validator rule on single-word flashcard answers.

findings.claim: Diffraction is taught in the article, restated in a Key Fact, tested by a 3-mark practice question and by a flashcard.
findings.truth: Diffraction does not appear anywhere in this specification. The physics as written is correct, so nothing is wrong; it is extra load and a practice question that could not be set on this course. Removing the practice question would be a judgement call for Tom rather than a fact fix.
findings.evidence: grep of the spec for 'diffract' returns no hits.

findings.claim: A collapsible teaches the transformer turns-ratio equation Vp/Vs = Np/Ns, a flashcard asks students to name it, and 4-mark practice question 4 requires it (500 turns primary, 50,000 turns secondary, 400 V in, 40,000 V out).
findings.truth: The turns-ratio equation is not in this specification. The only transformer relationship listed is Vp x Ip = Vs x Is (P3.3.5), and it sits in the 'select from a list and apply' table, so it is given to the student rather than recalled. The article does state Vp x Ip = Vs x Is correctly, and the arithmetic in the turns-ratio question is right (50,000 / 500 = 100; 400 x 100 = 40,000 V). Options: (a) leave the collapsible as enrichment but replace practice question 4 with one built on Vp Ip = Vs Is; (b) leave as is. Recommend (a): the calculation is correct physics but is a task this board would never set, and rewriting one question is cheap.
findings.evidence: spec 5h table (b), reference P3.3.5; the equations list contains no turns-ratio entry.

findings.claim: A worked example and 4-mark practice question 4 calculate branch currents in parallel circuits.
findings.truth: This specification keeps quantitative circuit work in series circuits and treats parallel circuits qualitatively. The physics and the arithmetic are correct (10/6 = 1.67 A, 10/4 = 2.5 A, 12/8 = 1.5 A, 12/4 = 3 A), and applying V = IR to one branch is defensible, so this is recorded rather than edited.
findings.evidence: spec P3.1.4a 'in d.c. series circuits'; P3.2.3 'qualitative only'; P3.2.4 'resistors in series'.

findings.claim: "You need to know the shapes for three key components" (ohmic resistor, filament lamp, diode).
findings.truth: The spec names four for I-V characteristic work: lamps, diodes, LDRs and thermistors. The LDR and thermistor shapes are not standard graph questions, so this is under-stated rather than wrong.
findings.evidence: spec P3.1.6b.

findings.claim: The Key Fact carrying F = BIl, and the two section headings 'The Motor Effect' and "Fleming's Left-Hand Rule", sat outside the `higher-only` wrappers that cover the paragraphs beneath them.
findings.truth: Topic P3.5 is bold in its entirety, narrative and all four outcomes, and F = BIl is bold in the equations list. The Key Fact is now wrapped and the two headings moved inside their existing wrappers, so a Foundation reader no longer meets a heading with nothing under it followed by a Higher-tier equation.
findings.evidence: bold spec P3.5 (whole topic bold); spec 5h table (b), P3.5.3 bold.

findings.claim: Practice questions 3, 4 and 6 test Fleming's left-hand rule, F = BIl and the simple electric motor with no tier tag.
findings.truth: All three sit in P3.5, which is Higher tier only. Prefixed '(Higher tier)'. The arithmetic was checked and is correct: F = 0.5 x 3 x 0.2 = 0.3 N, doubling the current gives 0.6 N.

findings.claim: Knowledge checks 1, 2 and 4 test Fleming's left-hand rule, the motor-effect force on a parallel conductor, and the split-ring commutator, with no tier tag.
findings.truth: All sit in P3.5, Higher tier only. Prefixed '(Higher tier)'. Knowledge check 5 (the match) was left alone: two of its three pairs are P3.4 content assessed at both tiers, so tagging the whole question would wrongly mark permanent magnets and electromagnets as Higher.
findings.evidence: bold spec P3.5.

findings.claim: Six flashcards test P3.5 content (F = BIl, the thumb in Fleming's rule, the three factors in the motor effect, the split-ring commutator, magnetic flux density, and the motor effect itself) with no tier tag.
findings.truth: Tagged '(Higher tier)' at the end of each question, per the flashcard convention.
findings.evidence: bold spec P3.5.

findings.claim: Two Key Takeaways, the exam tip and the 'Real-World Applications' paragraph all carry P3.5 content (F = BIl, Fleming's rule, the split-ring commutator, the motor effect behind loudspeakers) outside any `higher-only` wrapper.
findings.truth: These sit outside the wrappers and cannot be wrapped: a higher-only div cannot legally sit inside the takeaways list. Coordinator ruling 5 Sep: tag in place and accept the re-narration. The two takeaways that carry P3.5 content (n31 motor effect and F = BIl, n32 Fleming's left-hand rule and the split-ring commutator) now open '(Higher tier)'; the first takeaway is P3.4 and is left alone. The exam tip, which is built entirely on P3.5, gains an opening sentence saying the material is Higher tier only. The 'Real-World Applications' paragraph (n26) is left as written: loudspeakers and MRI scanners are P3.4 Ideas-about-Science context and only mention the motor effect in passing.
findings.evidence: bold spec P3.5; lesson conclusion_html n31/n32, exam_tip_html n28, content_html n26.

findings.claim: The unit is named 'physics-paper-1' and its eight lessons are split as if the board ran two physics papers.
findings.truth: This board runs ONE physics paper. Foundation: Biology /01, Chemistry /02, Physics /03, each 95 marks, 1 hour 45 minutes, 26.4% of the GCSE; the fourth paper /04 assesses all content, 75 marks, 1 hour 45 minutes, 20.8%. Higher mirrors this as papers 5 to 8. The physics paper assesses chapters P1 to P6 plus BCP7 and BCP8. Verified lesson-to-chapter mapping for this unit: L1 = P1.1 (with P5.1/P5.2 material, see F4), L2 = P1.2, L3 = P1.3 plus P1.1 spectrum outcomes, L4 = P2.1 and P2.2, L5 = P2.2 with P3.3.5/P3.3.6, L6 = P3.1 and P3.2, L7 = P2.1, P2.2.6 and P3.3, L8 = P3.4 and P3.5. So the unit covers chapters P1, P2 and P3 and its running order is sound. No lesson states a paper structure, number of papers, duration or mark total anywhere, so there is nothing to correct in the lesson text and no Gateway wording was found. Recommend leaving the unit names alone, as instructed, and treating the split as teaching order rather than an exam claim.
findings.evidence: spec Assessment Overview, Foundation and Higher tables; verified in the spec today.

findings.claim: Outcomes inside the covered chapters (P1 to P3) that no lesson in this unit teaches.
findings.truth: Practical work is the gap. Missing: the ripple-tank measurement of speed, frequency and wavelength, measuring refraction through a prism and investigating reflection off a plane mirror (all PAGP4, outcomes P1.3.7 and P1.3.8b/c); the resistance-of-a-wire experiment and its circuit diagram (P3.1.4b, PAGP6); the I-V characteristic experiments for lamps, diodes, LDRs and thermistors (P3.1.6b, PAGP6); investigating bulb brightness in series and parallel circuits (P3.2.2b, PAGP6); and circuit symbols and the positive/negative terminal convention (P3.1.7). Chapters P4, P5 and P6 are out of this unit's scope and science-ocr-b/physics-paper-2 is still queued, so they are not gaps. Note that these are Practical Activity Groups (PAGs), not 'required practicals'. No less than 15% of the written-paper questions assess practical skills, so this is a real hole. Options: (a) add a practical-skills lesson or a practical panel to L3 and L6; (b) accept and cover it in the revision guides. Recommend (a) for L6 at least, since PAGP6 carries three separate outcomes.
findings.evidence: spec P1.3.7, P1.3.8b/c, P3.1.4b, P3.1.6b, P3.1.7, P3.2.2b; PAG tables P4 Waves and P6 Circuits; 'No less than 15% of the questions will assess practical skills'.

summary: Eight lessons checked against chapters P1 to P3. Every worked example, mark-scheme calculation and answer key recomputed clean (wave speed, efficiency, kWh cost, V = IR, P = VI, P = I2R, transmission losses, F = BIl); the real damage was three CH2-for-methane errors in Lesson 2, a Key Fact in Lesson 1 that taught UV as non-ionising against P1.1.7c, and tier wrappers pointing the wrong way in Lessons 2, 3 and 8. No banned strings, no Gateway wording, no invented scientists and no placeholder questions.
